## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dubbalakaṭṭhajātaka* (Ja 105) is a short narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon, titled in English translation as *The Weak Branch*. In the commentary edited by V. Fausböll, the narrative begins with the verse opening *Bahum petam vane katthan ti* [Fausböll 1877]. The frame story recounts that while residing at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, the Buddha told this tale concerning a monk who had gone forth from a good family after hearing the Dhamma, yet lived in constant dread of death, terrified by every rustling wind or falling twig [Fausböll 1877].

In the story of the past, an elephant escapes from captivity into the Himalayan forests because it can no longer bear the agony of being broken and fettered [Sahni 2008]. Even in the wilderness, the elephant trembles in fear at minor disturbances until an arboreal deity (*rukkhadevatā*) counsels it to master its groundless panic [Sahni 2008; Fausböll 1877]. Pragati Sahni observes that this Jātaka is notable as perhaps the only story in the collection that explicitly acknowledges the pain and suffering that elephants endure during the breaking process [Sahni 2008]. Upon hearing the teaching, the fearful monk attained stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), and the Buddha revealed that he had been the tree deity, while the monk had been the runaway elephant [Fausböll 1877].
